problem: Prior embodied rearrangement benchmarks (Habitat 2.0, VRR, Transport Challenge, BEHAVIOR) give an explicit geometric, episodic or predicate goal. None require the agent to infer where objects belong. Prior human-preference or commonsense work is limited to table-tops or shelves, a single scene, few objects, or static text datasets with no embodied, partially observed house.
motivation: Writing an explicit goal for 'tidy the house' is impractical: it would need a rule for every object. A household robot should instead use commonsense about human placement preferences, including for novel objects it has never seen. LLMs trained on web text may hold this physical commonsense, but no benchmark tested this inside a partially observed, embodied house-scale rearrangement task.
key_idea: Build a crowd-sourced dataset of where humans consider objects misplaced or correctly placed in each room and receptacle, and use it to define an instruction-free house-tidying benchmark. As a baseline, pair a RoBERTa-embedding ranker, fine-tuned contrastively to score P(room|object) and P(receptacle|object,room), with frontier exploration and classical navigation/pick-place in a hierarchical modular agent.
insight: Commonsense ranking is the main bottleneck, and errors compound across the 3-5 rearrangements per episode. With oracle exploration, swapping the oracle ranker for the LLM ranker drops OS from 1.00 to 0.44 and ES from 1.00 to 0.04, roughly OS^4. Zero-shot MLM prompting of RoBERTa is no better than random (ORR mAP 0.42 vs 0.46 on test-unseen). A small MLP contrastively fine-tuned on only ~40% of objects transfers to unseen object categories (ORR mAP 0.81 test-unseen; embodied OS drops only 0.30→0.23 and SOS 0.39→0.36 from seen to unseen). Exploration is the second bottleneck: oracle ranker + frontier gives OS 0.64, and frontier beats random/forward-right (val OS 0.26 vs 0.12/0.11). Longer upfront exploration (n_e=512) raises object coverage but gives the worst OS; n_e=16 is best.
method: Human-preference dataset: 372 MTurk annotators, 10 annotations per object-room pair (268 categories × 17 room types). Each annotator sorts every receptacle into correct / misplaced / implausible and ranks them. A placement is correct (or misplaced) if more than 50% of annotators say so.

Mapping: builds a top-down allocentric map from depth + camera projection. GT semantic/instance masks localize objects and receptacles; a GT relationship sensor and a receptacle-room map record which object sits on which receptacle in which room.
Exploration: frontier-based exploration (Yamauchi; implementation of Ramakrishnan et al. 2020), run for n_e=16 steps whenever no rearrangement is pending.

LLM Ranker: P(receptacle,room|object) = P(room|object) [OR] × P(receptacle|object,room) [ORR]. Averaged last-layer RoBERTa-base embeddings of prompts like '<object> in <room>' feed a 3-layer MLP. ORR is trained with a contrastive (InfoNCE) loss; OR is trained with BCE over multiple valid rooms. Training uses only seen-split objects.

Misplacement classification: the ORR score is thresholded at s_L, chosen by F1 grid search on val. Correct receptacles are ranked by room order, then receptacle score, with incorrect receptacles appended last.

Planner: explores for n_e steps, re-scores all discovered object-receptacle pairs with the ranker, then executes rearrangements in discovery order (nav to object → pick → nav to receptacle → place). This loop continues until the step budget is used up.
Navigation + pick-place: map-based point navigation. The agent turns and pitches its head until the target instance ID is in view, then fires the magic-pointer interact action (1.5 m raycast).

setting.backbone: RoBERTa-base (frozen embeddings) + 3-layer MLP ranker trained with contrastive/BCE loss; classical frontier exploration, mapping and navigation (no learned policy)
setting.training_data: Housekeep human-preferences dataset restricted to seen-split objects (~40% of objects; 8 high-level categories), trained 1000 epochs; no RL/IL training of the embodied agent
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (128×128, 90° FoV) on Fetch head camera + GT semantic & instance segmentation + GT object-on-receptacle relationship sensor + receptacle→room map
setting.action_space: discrete: FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN base ±10°, head pitch ±10°, magic-pointer INTERACT (pick/place via 1.5 m raycast)
setting.privileged: GT semantic + instance segmentation, GT relationship (object-on-receptacle) sensor, GT receptacle-room mapping (pose presumably GT for mapping); oracle variants additionally use GT human preferences or a complete map

numbers_note: All metrics except MC are printed as fractions in [0,1] with standard errors. Per the formatting rules they are scaled ×100 here (e.g. OS 0.30 → 30, mAP 0.81 → 81). MC is already printed in %. Standard errors are omitted. Housekeep has test-seen and test-unseen splits; 'test' is used here for test-seen. The oracle-ranker + oracle-exploration upper-bound rows are omitted: ES 1.00, OS 1.00, SOS 0.65/0.64, RQ 0.63/0.61 on seen/unseen. The exploration-step (n_e) ablation is described only in text (n_e=16 best; n_e=512 gives OC 80% but the worst OS), and ES@K appears only in a figure. It is unclear whether the val-split ablation tables use val-seen or val-unseen. No external embodied baselines were evaluated, since this is a new benchmark.
results: The fully non-oracle modular baseline (RoBERTa+CM ranker + frontier exploration) reaches OS 0.30 on test-seen and 0.23 on test-unseen, but episode success is only 0.01 because errors compound across rearrangements. Oracle ranking + frontier exploration reaches ES 0.35 / OS 0.64, and LLM ranking + oracle map reaches OS 0.44, so both reasoning and exploration are bottlenecks. On the offline ranking task, RoBERTa+CM (ORR mAP 0.81, OR 0.65 on test-unseen) far exceeds zero-shot MLM prompting (0.42/0.52) and random (0.46/0.59). T5-base+CM is better still (0.84/0.68).
limitations: Relies on privileged GT semantic/instance segmentation, a GT object-on-receptacle relationship sensor, a receptacle→room map, and magic-pointer manipulation. The perception and manipulation challenges are therefore abstracted away.
Episode success is near zero (0.01). Exploration maximizes map coverage rather than task-driven object coverage, and the ranker has poor precision/recall at identifying which objects are misplaced.
The LLM is used only as a frozen embedding extractor with a small MLP (RoBERTa-base, 125M). No generative LLM planning is tried, and no end-to-end learned RL/IL agent is compared.
